title: Daily to monthly
objectives: Resample prices to a lower frequency and choose the right aggregation.
Compute monthly returns from daily closes.

screens.title: One close per month
screens.prose: A short extract of daily prices in £: a few days either side of each month end. A monthly chart needs one close for each month.
screens.question: Tap the close that should stand for February.

hints.text: A month's close is the price when the month ends.
Find the last trading day of February 2024. It was a leap year.
29 February closed at 12.25.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the last close inside February.

byKey.first: That is the first close of February. The month's close is where it ended, not where it began.
byKey.leap: 2024 is a leap year, so February ran to the 29th. Its last close is 12.25.
byKey.march: 1 March is already the next month.

explain.text: A monthly close is the last daily close in the month. February 2024 ended on the 29th, at 12.25. Anything in between is a daily wiggle the monthly chart leaves out.

screens.title: Monthly buckets
screens.prose: `df.resample("ME")` drops each row into a bucket for its calendar month. `"ME"` means month end. Move the slider to light up each bucket and read its label.
screens.question: What date labels March's bucket?

options.text: 2024-03-31, the last day of the month

options.why: The label is the calendar month end. 31 March 2024 was a Sunday, and pandas still uses it.
`"ME"` labels each bucket with its month end. `"MS"` would use the month start.
The index stays a date index, so every label is a full date.

hints.text: Set the slider to March and read the caption.
The last row in March is 28 March, but the caption shows another date.

feedback.correct: Buckets are labelled by calendar month end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the label in the caption with the slider on March.

explain.text: Each bucket gets the last calendar day of its month, even a Sunday. The rows inside keep their own dates. Good Friday, 29 March, simply has no row.

screens.title: Resampling
screens.prose:
Changing the frequency of a time series is **resampling**. Each bucket needs a rule for turning its rows into one value.

```python
vol = df["volume"].resample("ME").sum()
print(vol.loc["2024-02"].iloc[0])
```
screens.question: What does it print?

hints.text: `sum` adds every volume in the bucket.
February's bucket holds four rows.

feedback.correct: 63,000 shares traded in these February rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the four February volumes.

byKey.last: That is the volume on 29 February alone. `sum` adds the whole bucket.
byKey.mean: That is the average day. `sum` gives the month's total.
byKey.all: You added every row. Only the February bucket counts.

explain.text: `resample("ME").sum()` adds each month's volumes. Volume is a flow: shares traded over the month add up. Closes are levels, so they need a different rule.

screens.title: A monthly bar
screens.prose:
A monthly price bar has an open, a high, a low, a close and a volume. Each column needs its own rule.

```python
bars = df.resample("ME").agg({
    "open": ..., "high": ..., "low": ...,
    "close": ..., "volume": ...})
```
screens.question: Drag a rule onto each column.

hints.text: Each rule should say what the month did, as one bar.
The month opens at its first open and closes at its last close.
open: first, high: max, low: min, close: last, volume: sum.

feedback.correct: first, max, min, last and sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each column means for the whole month.

byKey.mean: No column of a bar is an average. The close is the last price, not the typical one.
byKey.first: `first` belongs to the open: the month opens where its first day opened.
byKey.last: `last` belongs to the close: the month closes where its last day closed.
byKey.sum: Only volume adds up. Prices are levels, so adding them means nothing.

explain.text: February opens at 12.07, reaches 12.45, dips to 12.04 and closes at 12.25 on 63,000 shares. Prices take first, max, min and last; the flow, volume, takes the sum.

screens.title: The average month
screens.prose:
A colleague computes monthly returns like this.

```python
m = df["close"].resample("ME").mean()
ret = m.pct_change()   # February: 0.0124
```
screens.question: What was February's return, from January's last close to February's? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Use the two month-end closes.
January ended at 12.05 and February at 12.25.

feedback.correct: 0.0166 from close to close, not the colleague's 0.0124.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide February's last close by January's last close.

byKey.mean: That is the colleague's number. It compares average prices, 12.285 against 12.135, which no investor could have traded at.
byKey.first: You stopped at February's first close, 12.18. The return runs from January's last close to February's last, 12.25.
byKey.back: You divided January by February. The later close goes on top.

explain.text: A holder from 31 January to 29 February earned $12.25 / 12.05 - 1 = 0.0166$. The mean blends prices from across each month, so its changes are smoothed and lagged. Use `last` for closes.

screens.title: A month with no rows
screens.prose:
This file has closes in January and March, and none in February.

```python
days = pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-31", "2024-03-28"])
s = pd.Series([10.00, 11.00], index=days)
print(s.resample("ME").last())
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: `resample` makes a bucket for every month in the range, empty or not. February is there, holding NaN.
`last` does not carry January's close forward. An empty bucket has no last value, so it is NaN.
pandas does not invent a 0. An empty bucket holds NaN.

hints.text: Does February get a bucket?
Buckets cover every month from the first row to the last.
February's bucket is empty, so its last value is NaN.

feedback.correct: An empty month still gets a row, holding NaN.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every month in the range gets a bucket.

explain.text: The buckets run from January to March, one per month. February's is empty, so `last` gives NaN. Decide what that means before computing returns: a missing file, or a halted stock.

screens.title: Resampling, in one place
screens.prose:
A monthly return runs from one month-end close to the next.

$$R_m = \frac{P_m}{P_{m-1}} - 1, \quad P_m = \text{last close in month } m$$

```python
me = df["close"].resample("ME").last()
ret_m = me.pct_change()          # first month NaN
vol_m = df["volume"].resample("ME").sum()
bars = df.resample("ME").agg({"open": "first",
    "high": "max", "low": "min",
    "close": "last", "volume": "sum"})
```
screens.question: Daily closes run from January to June. How many monthly returns are not NaN?

options.why: Six months give six month-end closes, but January has no earlier close to compare with.
Only the first month lacks a return. February to June give five.
After resampling there is one row per month, so there are six closes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the month-end closes, then lose the first.

explain.text: Six months give six month-end closes. Each return needs the month before it, so January's is NaN and five remain.

screens.title: Monthly returns for a report
screens.prose: A fund report shows monthly returns. `close` holds daily closes in £ with dates as the index. Return each month's return from month-end closes, rounded to 6 places, without the first month, which has no return.

params.xLabel: Every third trading day, January to April 2024

screens.question: Complete `monthly_returns(close)`.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on daily closes over 3 or 4 months, one newest first. Values must match exactly after rounding to 6 places. The first run loads pandas, which can take ten seconds or more; later runs are quick.

hints.text: Two steps: month-end closes, then returns between them.
`close.resample("ME").last()` gives one close per month.
`ret = me.pct_change()`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the bucket rule and when you take returns.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has four months, so three returns. If the numbers are close but not equal, check you used `last`, not `mean`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 expects `[0.016598, 0.033469]`. Daily returns resampled with `sum` or `mean` give other numbers: resample the closes first.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. `me` should come from `close.resample("ME")`.

explain.text: Resample the levels, then take returns: February is $12.25 / 12.05 - 1 = 0.016598$. Adding daily returns instead ignores compounding, and averaging closes blurs the month ends.

ideas: `resample("ME")` puts each row in a bucket for its calendar month, labelled by the month end. Every month in the range gets a bucket, even an empty one.
Each column needs its own rule: prices take `first`, `max`, `min` and `last`; volume, a flow, takes `sum`.
Monthly returns: resample the closes with `last`, then `pct_change()`. The first month is NaN.

formula.name: Monthly return
formula.note: $P_m$ is the last close in month $m$, from `resample("ME").last()`.

summary.trap: Averaging closes with `mean` before `pct_change` compares prices nobody could trade at. Use `last`.

quiz.prose: You resample daily data to weeks with `resample("W-FRI")`.
quiz.question: Which rule gives the shares traded in each week?

options.why: That is Friday's volume alone. The week's volume adds every day's.
That is the average day's volume, a fifth of the weekly total in a full week.
That is the busiest day. The week traded every day's shares.

feedback.correct: Volume is a flow, so it adds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shares traded on each day all count towards the week.

explain.text: Volumes count shares changing hands, so a week's total is the sum of its days. Closes are levels, so they take `last`.

quiz.prose: A stock's month-end closes were £50.00 in January and £52.00 in February. Its average close in February was £51.50.
quiz.question: What was February's monthly return? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the two month-end closes.
